summary: A country in northeastern Africa where the Blue Nile and White Nile meet at the capital Khartoum; it has more ancient pyramids than Egypt (in Nubia), shrank in area after South Sudan's independence in 2011, and has been in civil war since 2023.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest of Egypt in the 7th century, Islam began to seep southward; in 652 the Arabs and the Christian kingdom of Nubia signed the 'Baqt treaty', which maintained peaceful trade for hundreds of years as Arab tribes and merchants gradually moved south. In 1504 the Funj Sultanate was founded and converted to Islam, and Sufi orders then penetrated popular life, while the Christian kingdoms of Nubia fell one after another in the 14th to 16th centuries. In 1881 the Mahdist uprising established an Islamic state, and in 1983 the Nimeiry government imposed Islamic law. After the independence in 2011 of South Sudan, whose population is mainly Christian and traditional believers, the Muslim share of Sudan rose to more than ninety percent.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Christianity was introduced to Nubia from Byzantium in the 6th century, and the Nubian kingdoms followed Christianity for nearly a thousand years, leaving mural remains such as those of the Faras Cathedral. During the Anglo-Egyptian condominium of the late 19th century (1899–1956), missionaries operated mainly in the south, while missionary work in the north was restricted. After South Sudan's independence in 2011, the Christians remaining in Sudan are mainly minorities of the Nuba Mountains and Blue Nile State, as well as Copts and South Sudanese in the capital.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs exist mainly in border regions such as the Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan and Blue Nile State, where peoples preserved their own ancestral and nature beliefs during the process of Islamization. After South Sudan's independence in 2011, most of the population following traditional religions was counted in South Sudan, so their share in Sudan dropped sharply.

religion.background: Northern Sudan was the site of ancient Nubia and the Kingdom of Kush, and in the 6th century the Nubian kingdoms converted to Christianity. After the 7th century the Arabs gradually moved south, and after the founding of the Funj Sultanate in 1504 Islam became the mainstream, with Sufi orders having far-reaching influence. In 1881 the Mahdist uprising established an Islamic state, and from 1899 the country was under Anglo-Egyptian rule. After independence, religious differences between north and south triggered a long civil war; after South Sudan's independence in 2011, Sudan became a predominantly Muslim country.

language.official: The official languages are Arabic and English.

ranking.name: Arabic (Sudanese dialect)
ranking.description: Arabic entered Sudan after the 7th century with the southward movement of Arab tribes, and after hundreds of years of intermarriage and Islamization, the Nubians and other peoples of the north and center gradually switched to speaking Arabic. Sudanese Arabic dialect is centered on Khartoum, is the common language of the country, and is the language of government and education. Successive governments after independence pursued Arabization policies, making Arabic the mother tongue or second language of the great majority.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English was the language of administration and education during the Anglo-Egyptian condominium of 1899–1956, especially in the south, where Britain promoted English education through mission schools. After independence the government pursued Arabization and the status of English declined. The 2005 peace agreement made English co-official with Arabic, but after South Sudan's independence in 2011 the population that uses English as its main language fell sharply, and today it is mainly used in higher education and international exchanges.

language.history: Northern Sudan used Meroitic in ancient times, and the medieval Nubian kingdoms used Old Nubian, written in the Coptic alphabet. After the 7th century Arabic gradually spread south, and in the Funj Sultanate period it became the mainstream. During the Anglo-Egyptian condominium of 1899–1956, English became the administrative language. After independence the government pursued Arabization, provoking a backlash among peoples of the south. Today Sudan still has more than a hundred ethnic languages, such as Nubian, Beja and Fur.

ranking.name: Ful medames (stewed fava beans)
ranking.description: Fava beans are slowly simmered overnight over low heat until soft, then mashed, drizzled with sesame oil or olive oil, and mixed with cumin, salt, onion, tomato, white cheese or boiled egg, and eaten with bread.
ranking.history: Ful medames originated in ancient Egypt, where the inhabitants of the Nile valley were already growing fava beans thousands of years ago, and it spread up the Nile to Sudan. In Sudan, ful is the most common breakfast and lunch, and shops selling ful can be seen everywhere on the streets of Khartoum; workers and students often share a large plate together at the 'brunch' time (futur) around ten in the morning.

ranking.name: Kisra (sorghum flatbread)
ranking.description: Sorghum flour is mixed with water and fermented overnight, then spread on a heated iron griddle into extremely thin flatbreads, with a soft texture and a slight sourness, eaten with stews or okra soup.
ranking.history: Sorghum originated in Africa, and the area of Sudan and Ethiopia is one of the earliest places where it was domesticated; it is still Sudan's most important food crop. Kisra is a traditional staple of northern and central Sudan, requires skill to make, and traditionally is made by the women of the household every morning. It is similar to Ethiopia's injera, reflecting a shared food culture of northeastern Africa.

ranking.name: Asida (porridge dough)
ranking.description: Sorghum flour or wheat flour is poured into boiling water and stirred constantly, cooked into a thick lump, and eaten with meat sauce, okra soup or yogurt sauce.
ranking.history: Asida is a traditional dish shared by Sudan, the Arabian Peninsula and North Africa, and in Sudan it is most commonly made from sorghum. It is closely tied to Sudan's religious festivals and is common at the iftar meal during Ramadan and at Eid al-Fitr, and women who have just given birth also eat asida to regain strength. It is simple and filling, and is the everyday staple of rural Sudanese families.

ranking.name: Ta'amiya (fava bean fritters)
ranking.description: Soaked fava beans or chickpeas are ground, mixed with onion, garlic, coriander and spices, shaped into small patties and deep-fried, crisp outside and soft inside, often eaten stuffed into bread together with ful.
ranking.history: Ta'amiya is generally thought to have originated in Egypt, where ancient Coptic Christians made fava bean fritters as a meat substitute during fasting periods. It spread up the Nile to Sudan, and is called 'ta'amia' in both Sudan and Egypt. It is the most common street breakfast snack in Khartoum, cheap, and often combined with ful to make an ordinary person's breakfast.
ranking.imageCredit: Popo le Chien・CC BY-SA 3.0・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Karkadeh (hibiscus drink)
ranking.description: Dried hibiscus calyces are steeped in hot water and sweetened with sugar, and can be drunk hot or chilled, deep red in color and sweet and sour in taste; it is Sudan's most common traditional drink.
ranking.history: Hibiscus originated in Africa, and Sudan is an important hibiscus-producing country worldwide, especially in the western regions of Kordofan and Darfur. Karkadeh has a long history of being drunk in Sudan and Egypt and is especially popular in hot weather. During Ramadan, karkadeh is an essential drink for breaking the fast, and it is also used to serve guests at celebrations such as weddings.
